'AI everywhere,' said leadership. 'Everywhere but our data,' said infosec. Sitting between that, as a CPO, is a genuinely frustrating place to be.

But actually, I find this frustration one of the more useful diagnostics in the market right now.

AI is built for speed, Enterprise AI is built for control. Many vendors in the market right now are selling the first kind and calling it the second. 

The question here isn't how to get infosec to say yes to the shiny new AI solution, but whether you're asking for Enterprise AI in the first place. 

The demo looks the same either way. The architecture underneath doesn't.

The vendors who've built the enterprise layer with governance, controls, data confidentiality tend to get through. The ones who haven't, don't. We built that enterprise layer 22 years ago on the data side, and I find the same logic applies to every technology that eventually touches enterprise data. 

But CPOs who learn to make that distinction now will find themselves nodding a lot less and asking a lot more!

You can have the talent, the timing, the capital, the product. None of that matters if you need the odds to be in your favor. 

The good news is Finland has never been great at reading the odds anyway.

French profile.
Dutch profile.
German profile.
Spanish profile.

Old services.
Outdated achievements.
Topics of my previous life that I no longer wanted to be known for.

With the introduction of LinkedIn's Interest Graph I realized something.
My profile was attracting confusion instead of clients.

So I made 3 instant changes.

• I deleted all second-language profiles and kept one English version.
• I removed roughly 50% of my old content and experience.
• I rewrote my headline, About section and work descriptions fully from the client perspective.

Not “what I did.”
But “how I help.”

Within 3 weeks my profile attracted far more relevant visitors and my content reach increased by 20-30%.

LinkedIn rewards clarity.
So does your human audience.

Most profiles don’t need more information.
They need less noise.

Embracing myself for 46 degrees here today outside Valencia. That means getting up at 6:00am, taking care of the animals (ducks, chickens, geese, pigs) and walking Siena 🐶.
 
Writing this post at 8:20am outside with the temperature already on 33 degrees, before heading back into the house and spending time with my beloved air-conditioning.
 
I'm privileged to live in the middle of nature in beautiful Spain, but last year forest fires came close to 15km from my house, we could see the flames at night on top of the mountains at the horizon.
 
The extreme heat makes me more aware of how surface and architecture can influence what we feel every single day.
 
Looking at my plot I have asphalt, dried grass, weeds, trees, buildings. It's a dance between shade and full exposure to sun.

This one photo (originally posted by Louis De Jaeger) says more than any climate report.
 
Same street. 
Same sun. 
Same moment. 
The only difference is what covers the ground.
 
Asphalt and brick soak up the sun all day, then radiate it back at us long into the night. This is the urban heat island effect, baked into how we build.
 
Trees don't just block sun. They actively cool the air by releasing water, like a natural air conditioner running for free.
 
We spend fortunes on air conditioning to fight a heat we designed into our cities. Meanwhile the cheapest, most beautiful cooling technology on earth grows from the ground and asks for almost nothing in return.
 
A city without trees is an oven. A city with trees is a refuge. 
 
Definitely going to plant some extra trees in autumn

PS: Let me know, how many degrees are you expecting and where?

items.content:
Trust isn't a decision your audience makes on purpose. It's a shortcut their brain takes to avoid risk. Understand this and you'll grow your impact.

Most people treat LinkedIn trust like a light switch.
 
Post → hope people believe you.
 
Unfortunately that's not how it works. The shortcut to avoid bad decisions fires in milliseconds, long before anyone reads your value proposition.
 
A few things happening in your reader's head, whether you're aware of it or not:
 
1. The halo effect.
   means they judge your credibility before they've read a single line, based purely on how your profile looks.
 
2. Specificity beats vagueness, every time. 
   Vague claims trigger skepticism. Specific claims (even small ones) trigger belief, because the brain trusts receipts more than promises.
 
3. Loss aversion is why a single thoughtful comment does more for your pipeline than five posts. 
   Rare reads as valuable, and most engagement on this platform is not rare.
 
4. And the mere-exposure effect explains why the fifth touchpoint lands and the first one doesn't. 
   Your reader isn't more convinced by then. They're just less afraid.
 
None of this happens by accident. It happens because trust is an integrated system with four moving parts, working in sequence, not in isolation.
 
I've been on the platform since 2005 and honestly over 95% of people over-invest in just one signle part of that system, ignore the rest, then wonder why visibility never turns into pipeline.
 
In the Carousel you'll find the 4 pillars to build trust on LinkedIn. 
Swipe through it and let me know which one needs more attention!

article.title: #66 The AI Slop Reach Penalty
article.subtitle: Richard van der Blom
article.linkLabel: Open article: #66 The AI Slop Reach Penalty by Richard van der Blom • 6 min read
article.description: Last week I broke a habit I'd kept unbroken since January, and the reason had nothing to do with laziness. My head was too full of new ideas to make r

items.content:
Two types of LinkedIn creators. Only one builds a brand that survives.
The Hype Guy vs. The Doom Guy. 

You probably know a Hype Guy. Every post is a win. 
Every client is thrilled. LinkedIn "loves" him.
 
Then we have the The Doom Guy. LinkedIn is broken. Reach is dead. 
He's burned out and telling you about it daily.
 
Both work short-term. Both quietly damage your brand long-term.
 
𝗟𝗲𝘁'𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝘀𝘆𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆, 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲:
 
1. Our feeds are already biased toward positivity. Across major platforms, 80–90% of posts lean positive, even when people are not that happy offline. Result: your "always winning" narrative stops feeling inspiring and starts feeling fake.
2. Vulnerability does create connection, but only in a specific form. Recent studies show people trust you most when you share past, mild vulnerabilities plus current competence. "I struggled with X, here is how I solved it, here is the system" beats both "I never struggle" and "I'm still drowning."
3. Extremes drive engagement, not authority. One large LinkedIn analysis found neutral or mixed-tone posts can drive up to 9x more meaningful engagement than overly positive ones, and negative posts often spark more comments than hype posts. But if all you post is outrage, people see you as entertaining, not as someone they'd pay.
 
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱:
 
Live in "everything is a success" mode, and short-term you get more likes, less friction, easier sponsor deals. Long-term you get less perceived authenticity and an audience that quietly doubts your numbers and your advice.
 
Live in "LinkedIn is evil, I struggle every day" mode, and short-term you get more comments, more debate, more "finally someone says it." Long-term you brand yourself as the system's victim, not the operator who can navigate it and help others win.
 
People follow success with scars. 
Not success without cracks. 
Not struggle without solutions. 
 
My recommendation: show wins with receipts. Show struggles with constraints. Stop performing at the extremes, and let your feed show competence and honesty instead of hype and drama.

Now! Audit your last 30 posts. Which extreme are you closer to, and what is that doing to how people trust your brand?

Note to myself: let's balance it a bit more okay Mr. Critical Guy?
PS: Bonus points for guessing the venue where this picture was taken.

items.content:
LinkedIn creators aren’t fighting the algorithm. 
They’re fighting 4 much bigger challenges.

If you’re posting consistently and still feel invisible, it’s probably not your “content quality”. 
Nope, I think it's the system you’re trying to win in.

4 Real challenges most LinkedIn creators are facing right now👇

1. Reach is collapsing while effort is exploding 
   You post more, you engage more… and your impressions still go down. The feed is overcrowded, attention is fragmented, and LinkedIn quietly prioritises formats that keep people scrolling and clicking, not thinking. Result: High‑effort posts get the same reach as low‑effort “engagement bait” and creators burn out.
   
2. The platform wants creators, but isn’t built for them 
   LinkedIn talks about “supporting creators”, but most tools still serve recruiters, advertisers and B2B sales teams first. External links are punished (don't tell me they aren't because some person at LinkedIn says they aren't), analytics are still pretty basic, and there’s no real creator‑centric infrastructure for audience ownership or monetisation. You’re building a brand on rented land, with very limited control over what gets seen and by whom.
   
3. Format shift is happening faster than skill shift 
   Carousel posts are no longer the default power format. Text only, video, visual storytelling and “multi‑touch” content loops win. In the meantime most creators still operate like it’s 2024. The gap between “I can write a post” and “I can architect a content system” is where a lot of reach and revenue is currently dying.
   
4. Engagement doesn’t equal business outcomes anymore 
   It’s now very possible to have big numbers and small pipelines. The feed rewards emotional stories, but most creators don’t have a clear path from post → profile → product → pipeline Likes, comments and followers feel good… until you realise they’re not paying your invoices.

If you’re creating content on LinkedIn please keep this in mind:
You don’t need more content. You need a better content economy around you:

• Clear positioning instead of random topics
• A portfolio of formats, not just text posts
• A distribution & relationship strategy beyond the feed
• A monetisation path that turns attention into opportunity
  
I’m curious: Which of these 4 challenges is hitting you the hardest right now—1, 2, 3 or 4?

Drop the number in the comments and I’ll reply with one practical fix you can implement this week.

items.content:
I never shared how much money I make. Not a single Stripe payout screenshot. Am I doing LinkedIn wrong?

Maybe it's my Dutch heritage.
We're the people who split restaurant bills down to the cent, but would rather die than tell you our salary.

Or maybe it's how I was raised.
I didn't know what my dad earned until I left the house at 23.
Money was discussed the same way we discussed feelings.
We didn't.

But apparently "sharing what you earn" is the new social proof.

Coaches flexing cohort sign-ups.
Screenshots of Stripe dashboards.
"How I made $847,293 in Q2" (oddly specific numbers = more believable, right?)

And here I am, still thinking social proof comes from clients and your network.
Like a caveman.

Then last month I lost a community member.
His reason, and I quote:

"The other guy made millions last year and can show me how to do it too."

My first instinct? Tell him what I earned.
My second instinct? Let him go find out what "made millions" actually means.

Maybe I'm old-fashioned.
Maybe I should start posting income screenshots.
Maybe I should buy a Lamborghini and pose next to it.

Or maybe I'll just keep building things that work.

What's your take,  does talking money prove success?
Or just prove you talk about money?

PS: Don't worry about me. I'm fine financially.

The algorithm is changing fast, so we stepped up the pace of our research as well. 5 Trends worth knowing, based on +12,000 creators since March.

The first one I noticed myself, down -22% for my own content.

1. Carousels are tanking.

Our analysis of 40,000+ carousel posts shows average reach is down 40%, and engagement has dropped by 30%. LinkedIn is making room for video, and your audience is done swiping through low-value slides.

2. Deleting posts hurts more than it helps.

Got a typo, wrong visual, or just underperforming content? Unless it's truly off-brand, let it live. Try to resuscitate it. Deleting doesn't erase it from your history; it signals instability to the algorithm.

3. Your connections are dragging down your reach.

Want to grow fast? Build followers. But be ruthless about who you connect with. If they don't post, don't engage, and sit outside your topic fingerprint, they'll quietly tank your distribution.

4. Spamming DMs is killing your visibility.

If people keep ignoring your messages, LinkedIn notices. Low response rates on your outbound DMs signal spam behavior, and the platform will suppress your profile and content. Honestly, I'm cheering for this one.

5. Comment-and-run is getting penalized.

Leave 30 comments and disappear? LinkedIn now tracks whether you follow up. If someone replies to your comment and you ghost them, our data shows your comment reach can drop by 35%. Your relevance ranking tanks.

The algorithm rewards behavior that looks like genuine participation.
Performative tactics are quietly dying, and honestly, that's a good thing!

items.content:
A member of my TRIBE community reached out last week. His DMs weren't getting any responses.
"Send them over" I said. He's making a mistake most of us make.
 
He was putting in real effort, thoughtful, well-intended messages. But without realizing it, every one of them was a statement about himself. His work, his offer, his value. Not one left room for the other person to say anything back.
 
That's not a copywriting problem but more a psychology problem.
 
Let me tell you what's actually happening in someone's head when they open a DM:
 
→ If the message asks them to justify their own behavior ("why did you view my profile?"), most people have no real answer, what do they reply? Right. Nothing! 
 
→ If the message describes you instead of them, there's nothing in it for their brain to react to.
 
→ If the message ends in a soft, open-ended CTA ("I'm just a DM away"), you've handed them all the work of deciding what happens next. Most people won't do that work. They'll just scroll on.
 
The fix isn't "be more salesy" or "be more casual." 

It's actually much more simple:
 
Every message should end in something answerable in under 10 seconds. 
A specific question. A fork. A light provocation instead of a statement.
 
I broke this down into the 3 moments that matter most:

1. Profile View
2. Connection request accepted
3. 48 Hours later

items.content:
Spent the last few weeks running experiments for the October Algorithm Report update. Three things stood out. All three surprised me.
 
1. "Celebrate an Occasion" posts get an algorithm boost
 
Bigger creators are quietly shifting their announcement content. Not "here's my new offer" but "I hit 25,000 followers." "I signed client #1,000." "I just became an ambassador for [tool]."
 
I was skeptical. Then I tested it myself. My own celebration post outperformed my regular announcement posts by 2.3x impressions.
 
Across 800 posts we analyzed, the average lift sits between 1.6x and 2.1x.
 
How to use it:
 
• Attach the milestone to a number, not a feeling. "25,000 followers" beats "grateful for this community."
• Pair the win with one specific lesson, not a thank-you list.
• Use it sparingly. This works because it's rare. Every week and it reads as humble-bragging, not milestone-marking.
 
2. Infographics are in freefall, especially AI-made ones
 
2024 was the year of the infographic. Dense visual, one scroll-stop, multiplier between 5x and 7x. Everyone piled in.
 
That era is over. Across more than 6,000 infographics we analyzed, the format now sits between 0.9x and 1.4x. Some underperform a plain text post. Fully AI-designed ones drop further, to 0.6x-1.1x.
 
My read: infographic fatigue plus a growing "this smells like plagiarism/AI" instinct from the audience.
 
What to do instead:
 
• Swap the single dense infographic for a document post (carousel/PDF). Underused, and it outperforms infographics at the moment
• One clear insight per visual, not ten data points crammed into one frame.
• Hand-drawn or clearly human-annotated visuals are currently beating polished AI graphics. Imperfection reads as authenticity.
 
3. Popular topics can pull you outside your own topic cluster
 
Your distribution is built mostly on topic fit now, not network size. Which normally means: stay in your lane, post your 2-3 core themes, let the algorithm learn where you belong.
 
But there's an exception. Tie a trending, seasonal topic to a genuine personal experience, and it temporarily pulls your post into interest clusters you don't normally reach. Summer is here, so climate and sustainability content is a live example. Across 1,200+ posts in this category, a post connecting that theme to a personal experience outperformed regular posts by up to 3.5x impressions.

How to use this: 

Treat it as an occasional excursion, not a new content pillar. The topic gets you the temporary reach into new clusters. Your usual 2-3 themes are what get you remembered once people arrive.
 
None of these samples come close to the 1.3 million posts behind the Algorithm Insights Report itself, but 800 to 6,000+ posts is still a solid early signal. Full breakdown lands in the October update.

items.content:
Gianni Infantino and the FIFA just gave every leader on this platform a live case study in how NOT to use power.
 
One phone call from the Oval Office. One suspended red card. One World Cup match reshaped in real time.
 
In case you didn't got the message.
 
Trump called Infantino. Asked him to review Balogun's suspension. Days later, FIFA suspended the automatic ban for a one-year probation. Belgium's appeal got thrown out on a technicality: apparently they weren't even a "party" to their own protest. The US played Belgium anyway.
 
Result? USA lost 4-1. Eliminated. Every ounce of "special treatment" backfired spectacularly.
 
But the damage was already done before kickoff.
 
UEFA called it "unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable." Belgium's federation said it was "astonished." Infantino kept insisting the judicial bodies are independent, while confirming on the record that a sitting head of state got a rule bent in his direction.
 
The leadership lesson hiding behind all of this?
 
Infantino's entire mandate after the Blatter scandals was one word: TRUST Show the world FIFA plays it straight, every time, for everyone.
 
He broke it in one weekend. In front of the biggest audience football has ever had.
 
Now let's bring this to LinkedIn.
 
You also have power. Reach. Authority. Followers who take your word more seriously than they probably should.
 
The temptation is the same one Infantino faced. Bend a rule. Make an exception. Protect someone close to you when you think nobody's watching.
 
Except on LinkedIn, everybody's watching.
 
Three rules I never break with influence, and what they look like on LinkedIn:
 
1. Protect fair process. 
   Don't quietly delete a critical comment on your own post because it makes you look bad. Leave it up, or reply to it in public.
   
2. Share the spotlight. 
   Don't claim your success when it's a joint effort like "I built this." Tag the people who actually did the work, in the post, not buried in a comment.
   
3. Set the standard higher. 
   Don't write a glowing recommendation for someone in your circle that you wouldn't write for a stranger with the same track record.
 
Infantino had one shot to prove FIFA earned trust back. 
He ruined it on a single phone call.
 
You get hundreds of those "one phone calls" a year, in comments, in promotions, in decisions nobody will ever audit.
 
What's the one rule you'd never bend, even for your favorite person in the room?

→ 3. Design a sustainable rhythm, not a heroic sprint.
Pick a narrow promise for your audience (aka one problem, one transformation) and show up consistently in that lane. Build recurring formats you can execute on autopilot instead of reinventing yourself every day for the feed.

LinkedIn 2027 will be brutal on people who still act like creators instead of operators.

items.content:
It was 1999. My first job, at a staffing agency. A major Dutch car factory put their staffing contract out to tender. 10 agencies invited to pitch, round one.
 
That got cut to 6, for round two.
 
Then 3 of us, for a final round: half a day of negotiation, brainstorming, and presentations to convince them we should be their primary supplier.
 
All human to human. Three rounds. Months of work. Not a single piece of it done online, no digital research, no shortlisting mechanisms, nothing like that.
 
That's how B2B used to work. People met people, and the best relationship-builder usually won the deal.
 
Fast forward to last week, when I watched two AI agents negotiate a vendor contract.
 
No human in the room. No human in the loop until the final sign-off. Pricing, terms, back-and-forth, all handled machine-to-machine, in about 4 minutes.
 
Same fundamental task as that car factory tender. Completely different world.
 
We've spent 25 years optimizing GTM for human attention (better copy, better design, better funnels, better "personalization.") All of it built on one assumption: a person reads it, feels something, decides.
 
That assumption is starting to break.
 
→ Discovery is moving from search and ads to protocol-native distribution agents can parse 
→ Trust is moving from brand and design to machine-readable reputation 
→ Funnels are becoming autonomous journeys, no human required to move stage to stage 
→ CRMs are turning from systems of record into systems of action 
→ Revenue itself is becoming a recursive execution loop, not a quarterly motion
 
Most of us are still optimizing for a buyer who reads, feels, and decides like I did in that boardroom in 1999.
 
The next buyer might not read at all.
 
I'm not saying humans disappear from B2B as high-stakes decisions still need someone accountable for them. I'm saying the 𝘱𝘢𝘵𝘩 to that decision is being rebuilt by agents, right now, while most of us are still A/B testing subject lines.
 
If that unsettles you a little good. 
It should have unsettled me too, watching that demo.

items.content:
Most companies are leaving 80% of their LinkedIn reach on the table. Not because they're inactive, but because they're following outdated rules.

They invest in the Company Page, hire someone to post 3x a week and then wonder why only 200 people see it.

Your Company Page and your personal profile aren't competitors.
You just need to treat them like a system, which most companies don’t understand.

After analysing millions of posts for the Algorithm Insights Report 2026, this is what we see at the moment:

→ 1. Personal profiles get 8x more reach and 12x the engagement of Company Pages
Pages speak into the void. People interact. If your team isn't posting, your brand is invisible.

→ 2. "Resharing with your own thoughts" is a "no-go"
LinkedIn classifies this as low-effort copied content and suppresses it. What works: comment on the Company Page post, or use instant reshare. Two actions. Completely different outcome.

→ 3. Your thought leaders are your highest-value distribution channel
B2B buyers follow people, not logos. Content from C-level profiles reaches a more relevant, more senior audience than brand content ever will.

items.content:
I called my dad yesterday for Father's Day. One day too late. He won't mind. In less than 3 months I will be a father myself. Exciting and terrifying at the same time.
 
Four years. Two lost pregnancies. Medical complications. Conversations late at night about whether to keep going, whether this was still worth it, whether we were still okay.
 
We kept going.
 
And now The Netherlands and Argentina are creating a little piece of Spain.
 
When I shared those experiences publicly, over 200 DMs came in. People I had never met, going through the same thing. Parents growing old and getting dementia. Miscarriages before becoming a father and mother. My wife read them with me. That moment reminded me why I talk about the hard stuff.
 
Same when I write about my dad's dementia. Him in the Netherlands, with me in Spain as an only child. My mom gone since last summer. It's not easy to put into words, but people care and respond, because they know there words might help to heal.
 
I was 27 when I met my ex-wife. She had two boys, three and seven years old. For seventeen years I tried to be a good stepfather. They taught me so many valuable lessons. Patience, presence, showing up even when you don't know if you're doing it right.
 
When I met Evelina in 2021, we knew early on what we both wanted. So we went all-in, but the road was harder than we expected.
 
September will change everything. Three of us. Four if you count Siena, our thirteen year old labradoodle who has no idea what is coming.
 
My dad? The thing about dementia nobody tells you, is that it sometimes comes with a laugh. Every time I remind him he is becoming a grandfather at 80, it is the first time he hears it. And every single time, he cannot stop cheering.
 
I get to give him that moment twice a day.
 
Life is not clean or linear. But it is worth showing up for.
 
Don't you think?
 
PS: We mixed up the football shirts in the photo. I should wear the Dutch one. Evelina the Argentinian. The little one gets the Spanish. We'll get it right in September. That's a promise.
